mechanics.name: Empower
mechanics.blurb: Put loyalty counters on a planeswalker token, creating it first if you don't have one. Five walkers, one per colour, and the archetypes are named for them.

quotes.name: Kiora of Salt and Sand
quotes.text: Since it doesn’t have an ability that lets you empower, this isn’t the best blue/green payoff in the world, but these 8/8 hexproof tokens should be more than enough to win a game if you can create even one.

quotes.name: Theorist's Proxy
quotes.text: The empower 3 allows you to draw a card, which already makes Theorist's Proxy comparable to something like a Spirited Companion , but the high toughness also makes it better at protecting your Jace token should you need to build it up for a bigger loyalty ability.

quotes.name: Way of the Healer
quotes.text: Way of the Healer starts out by giving you up to two 2/2s from the Jace token it creates, which will be better than drawing cards on average, but then it just sticks in play and makes every empower ability you use a lot stronger.

quotes.name: Rewrite Regrets
quotes.text: Rewrite Regrets might find a home in Reality Fracture thanks to the big landcycling creatures like Apex Witchstalker , especially since the empower ability is a nice bonus that other spells don’t normally give us.

quotes.name: Countersculpt
quotes.text: The empower 1 will usually result in a free surveil, like Sinister Sabotage , and if you can get the mana discount on it because you have a bunch of other empower sources then it just gets even better.

quotes.name: Fatehold Charm
quotes.text: When looking over these charms , I figured Fatehold Charm would probably have Consider as one of its modes, so the mode of drawing a card and empowering 2 is a very nice surprise.

mechanics.name: Prepared
mechanics.blurb: A creature that enters prepared carries a spell on its back: while it is prepared you may cast a copy of that spell, which unprepares it. Two cards in one, and the reason the reviewer keeps calling these cheap.

quotes.name: Prudent Fateseer
quotes.text: Most of the power behind Prudent Fateseer comes from the fact that it has Peer Review as a prepared spell, so it’s actually two creatures in one card, but I don’t give it much credit beyond that.

quotes.name: Master of Barbs
quotes.text: Normally, the ability on Master of Barbs would look kind of situational, but thanks to the Stingerquill prepared spell, Vicious Verse, there should actually be a lot of ways to trigger it.

quotes.name: Solarium Sentry
quotes.text: Most cards in your average Limited deck are going to cost more than 2 mana, but the prevalance of cheap prepare spells means Solarium Sentry will actually trigger a good bit.

quotes.name: Diviner of Victory
quotes.text: Between its own prepared spell, Jace tokens, and the Fatehold archetype as a whole, Diviner of Victory may be able to attack as a 3/3 or even a 4/4 on certain turns.

quotes.name: Semester Foreseer
quotes.text: Four mana for a 3/4 plus a surveil isn’t that good, but getting a free prepared spell out of it on a later turn, or perhaps the same turn, sounds really good.

quotes.name: Cruel Calculations
quotes.text: All you need to do is cast the Omit Variables prepared spell and this will draw you three cards, which is a great deal for 3 mana.

mechanics.name: Surveil
mechanics.blurb: Look at the top card, bin it or keep it. Selection that also fills a graveyard, which is why it turns up in both the white-blue aggro deck and the blue-black graveyard one.

quotes.name: Yuriko, Hope from the Shadows
quotes.text: Yuriko, Hope from the Shadows doesn’t do this particularly consistently, but it does also have the buyout of getting to surveil 2, which can also trigger Fatehold cards, so this ninja seems pretty good on balance.

quotes.name: Saheeli, Consul of Oversight
quotes.text: Creating a thopter token every time you scry or surveil is incredible in Fatehold, but it also synergizes incredibly with the Jace tokens, so it might just be good enough to top the curve in any white deck.

quotes.name: Countersculpt
quotes.text: The empower 1 will usually result in a free surveil, like Sinister Sabotage , and if you can get the mana discount on it because you have a bunch of other empower sources then it just gets even better.

quotes.name: Proft, Consulting Detective
quotes.text: If you’re drafting Fatehold and have plenty of ways to scry and surveil, then Proft, Consulting Detective is one of your best payoffs.

quotes.name: Proctor of Potential
quotes.text: It’s already great as a 2-drop 3/1 that surveils when it enters and can replay itself out of the graveyard, but then consider how it synergizes with other cards from this color pair.

quotes.name: Way of the Healer
quotes.text: As powerful as the empower mechanic can be, only getting to surveil or draw limits what the Jace tokens can do, so giving them better abilities sounds very lucrative.

mechanics.name: Legendary
mechanics.blurb: A third of the set. Named characters, many appearing twice in different colours, which is what makes 'every deck has a legend in it' a safe assumption here and a payoff worth building on.

quotes.name: Icy Reception
quotes.text: A Mana Leak that only hits creatures and legendary spells is still pretty strong, since that should be most of the cards your opponents will play in the first place.

quotes.name: Fateshaper Aspirant
quotes.text: I’d imagine that nearly every deck in this format will have at least one legendary creature in it, thanks to the prevalence of the echoed pairs.

quotes.name: Uldaros Theorix
quotes.text: All five of these legendary sphinxes are phenomenal cards and will all be great starts to any draft in this format.

quotes.name: Winter, Tormented Loner
quotes.text: This is a pretty good way to design a legendary Fleshbag Marauder .

quotes.name: Way of the Healer
quotes.text: This cycle of legendary enchantments is really intriguing.

themes.name: Format speed
themes.blurb: How quickly games end, and whether beating down beats building up.

quotes.name: Memory Trap
quotes.text: This is an early frontrunner for white’s best common, but even if it isn’t, it should still be a premium pickup when you’re drafting white.

quotes.name: Skilled Battlecarver
quotes.text: This is a very powerful 2-drop, but it’s best suited for aggressive decks, meaning it looks pretty mediocre in Konstrari builds.

quotes.name: Paradox Shaper
quotes.text: It even works well in the late game to restock your deck with some of your best cards and stop yourself from decking out.

quotes.name: Sphinx's Approach
quotes.text: I think this is quite playable in a slower control deck, but I’d never play it in an aggressive deck.

quotes.name: Hexhaven Battalion
quotes.text: This card looks amazing to me, and it’s my early pick for white’s best common.

quotes.name: Greenhouse Propagator
quotes.text: Turn 3 is definitely not my favorite time to be ramping , but Reality Fracture does look slow enough to accommodate that, and Soul Tether is also a 3-mana ramp spell, which leads me to believe this is actually what we’ll be doing in this set.

quotes.name: Aerid Konstrari
quotes.text: Aerid Konstrari isn’t only a beefy creature that can close out games, it also ramps you with a Heartwood token and then has an activated ability that not only creates more of them but also speeds up the clock and kills your opponent faster?

quotes.name: Marwyn, the Clearcutter
quotes.text: When you get to the late game, turning your Heartwood tokens and excess lands into more cards is something that should help you turn the corner, but only being a vanilla creature up to that point means it’s fairly limited in scope.

quotes.name: Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer
quotes.text: While you need to support it to maximize its potential, Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer is a very powerful and aggressive creature that demands an answer of some kind and even punishes chump blocks with its last ability.

quotes.name: Way of the Pyromancer
quotes.text: Of course, having your Jace token act as a mana dork is a lot worse than it being a creature, since it’s a lot more vulnerable, but with there being so few other ways to do this early, it should be worth the risk.

quotes.name: Splinter Twin
quotes.text: If you pick it up early in a draft, you could look for a copy or two of Divining Duelist and put together the classic auto-win that made this card the bane of every Modern player’s existence throughout the 2010s.

quotes.name: Afterthought Sentry
quotes.text: We never see colorless creatures of this size, so I’m interested to see how Afterthought Sentry plays out, but I’d imagine that aggressive decks will be able to find better options in their own colors.

quotes.name: Solarium Sentry
quotes.text: When you’re matched up against a deck like blue/red prowess though, its stock goes way up because now it should trigger off of most of their spells, making it incredibly hard for the opponent to race.

quotes.name: Hallway Heckler
quotes.text: Tacking on a Vicious Verse for free is nice, but decks that want that extra damage ping are probably going to want to be more aggressive than what a creature like Hallway Heckler is suited for.

themes.name: Removal
themes.blurb: How much interaction the set has and what it costs.

quotes.name: Vigorbloom Annex
quotes.text: As with all cycles of common dual lands , you should pick these up if you need fixing and prioritize them over medium-level commons, but not over premium cards like removal or the more powerful legends.

quotes.name: Stingcaster Mage
quotes.text: The best thing to do will typically be to flashback a removal spell and turn this into a makeshift Flametongue Kavu , but there are a lot of other options.

quotes.name: Teyo, Diamondblade Mage
quotes.text: Only giving a single +1/+1 counter and deathtouch isn’t the best trick in the world, and being only a 3/1 for 4 mana itself isn’t very impressive.

quotes.name: Last Gasp
quotes.text: For 2 mana, this is one of the most efficient removal spells in FRA, and it’ll probably be the best black common.

quotes.name: Teyo, Lightshield Expert
quotes.text: Some, like Shardmage's Rescue , provide some additional benefit beyond stopping a removal spell, but Teyo, Lightshield Expert not only gives a +1/+1 counter (or loyalty counter), but a whole body for you to use to your advantage.

quotes.name: Compel Brutality
quotes.text: You should be wary of black and red, as their removal spells are very good in Reality Fracture and they will have ways to disrupt this, but it’s still a strong card, especially when you pair it with a deathtouch creature.

quotes.name: Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer
quotes.text: While you need to support it to maximize its potential, Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer is a very powerful and aggressive creature that demands an answer of some kind and even punishes chump blocks with its last ability.

quotes.name: Perfected Theory
quotes.text: While costing 1 mana and having the flexibility to buff your own creature or downgrade your opponent’s, Perfected Theory is still just a combat trick in the color least likely to want one in the first place.

quotes.name: Multiply by Zero
quotes.text: It’s a perfect representation of the name and a very powerful removal spell, able to kill any creature that doesn’t have a toughness buff of some kind, and it can at least shrink those creatures in combat.

quotes.name: Verdant Kraken
quotes.text: If your opponent can’t answer it before their turn begins, you’re getting a minimum of a 3/3 out of the deal, and then even more if they still can’t find a way to remove it.

quotes.name: Emrakul, the Exigent Doom
quotes.text: I’m not saying Emrakul will be removed every time, but the fact that your opponent can deal with it is too much of a downside for me to want to go out of my way to play it.

quotes.name: Extended Absence
quotes.text: There’s a lot of good removal in Reality Fracture , but there’ll always be a need to cleanly remove anything, and the extra damage ping is very welcome in Stingerquill.

quotes.name: Hungering Puppetbeast
quotes.text: While I’m not ecstatic at the thought of losing my Heartwood tokens to fuel it, it’s so absurdly big and difficult to deal with that I don’t think I’ll care too much.

quotes.name: Pia, Aether Ascetic
quotes.text: You can’t always run Pia, Aether Ascetic , but this set has quite a few powerful enchantments, including the cycle of “Way” enchantments and multiple removal spells.

themes.name: Bombs and rares
themes.blurb: Cards that decide a game if nobody deals with them.

quotes.name: Aerid Konstrari
quotes.text: This card is absolutely incredible and a great first pick to cement you into what might be the best Hexhaven school.

quotes.name: Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer
quotes.text: While you need to support it to maximize its potential, Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer is a very powerful and aggressive creature that demands an answer of some kind and even punishes chump blocks with its last ability.

quotes.name: Gideon the Oathless
quotes.text: Although Gideon isn’t a huge bomb or anything, it seems to provide just enough to be a very annoying creature and a welcome addition to any deck, particularly aggressive ones.

quotes.name: Sanctum Lurker
quotes.text: Sanctum Lurker isn’t exactly a bomb rare, but it does provide a good amount of value and is a great addition to any deck with a good number of empower cards.

quotes.name: Kwia Vigorbloom
quotes.text: The Black Lotus tokens it creates are a funny touch, but really not necessary to make this one of the silliest bombs in the set.

quotes.name: Liliana the Faultless
quotes.text: While not a bomb rare by any means, there’s a lot to like on this Liliana, and it comes down as early as turn 1.

quotes.name: Denzilore Fatehold
quotes.text: This card is just obscene, and I can’t imagine being able to win the game against anyone who plays it right.

quotes.name: Verdant Kraken
quotes.text: This bomb rare is a reference to Verdant Force , an extremely powerful rare in its own right.

quotes.name: Uldaros Theorix
quotes.text: Our last sphinx and it’s still a massive bomb.

themes.name: Build-arounds
themes.blurb: Cards that do nothing alone and a lot with help.

quotes.name: Kiora of Salt and Sand
quotes.text: Since it doesn’t have an ability that lets you empower, this isn’t the best blue/green payoff in the world, but these 8/8 hexproof tokens should be more than enough to win a game if you can create even one.

quotes.name: Bloombrute
quotes.text: I often say that the best build around cards in Limited are usually the ones that draw a card whenever you do the thing, so of course I like Bloombrute .

quotes.name: Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer
quotes.text: While you need to support it to maximize its potential, Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer is a very powerful and aggressive creature that demands an answer of some kind and even punishes chump blocks with its last ability.

quotes.name: Saheeli, Consul of Oversight
quotes.text: Creating a thopter token every time you scry or surveil is incredible in Fatehold, but it also synergizes incredibly with the Jace tokens, so it might just be good enough to top the curve in any white deck.

quotes.name: Guiding Hydra
quotes.text: You obviously need a lot of creatures to make this work to its full potential, but white looks to be quite good at that in Reality Fracture , so I don’t see that I’d ever not want to play this card.

quotes.name: Danitha, Sword of Hope
quotes.text: Danitha, Sword of Hope isn’t supported well enough for you to consider it a solid build-around, but there are enough synergies that it should at least be a playable card in the right deck.

quotes.name: Chandra's Emberling
quotes.text: Some variants on this design have seen play in the past, but the difficulty is even wanting to put a comparatively weak creature in a deck that has enough noncreature spells to support it.

quotes.name: Proctor of Potential
quotes.text: It’s already great as a 2-drop 3/1 that surveils when it enters and can replay itself out of the graveyard, but then consider how it synergizes with other cards from this color pair.

quotes.name: Pompous Battlemage
quotes.text: Prowess is a supported archetype in Reality Fracture , with lots of good 1-mana spells to trigger them, but Pompous Battlemage feels a little too reserved for my liking.

quotes.name: Paradox Shaper
quotes.text: I’m very impressed with the amount of graveyard support there is in this set, and that makes me really happy to see an enabler as strong as this one.

quotes.name: Stinging Vitriol
quotes.text: Two mana is very reasonable for this effect, and you’ll always get the 2 damage out of it anyway, so it’ll also trigger your Stingerquill synergies.

quotes.name: Titanbones, Towering Heart
quotes.text: Titanbones, Towering Heart looks like an excellent payoff for Vigorbloom decks, and something I’d probably look to take early and try to make work.

quotes.name: Command the Stage
quotes.text: Unless you curve a 2-drop wizard into this, the first cast could be a little rough, but this still looks like an incredible card to build around.

quotes.name: Necrodominance
quotes.text: Triple black makes it too difficult to cast, and without the ability to also draft the right cards to support it, it just has too many downsides.

themes.name: Commons and filler
themes.blurb: The cards that actually make up the deck.

quotes.name: Vigorbloom Annex
quotes.text: As with all cycles of common dual lands , you should pick these up if you need fixing and prioritize them over medium-level commons, but not over premium cards like removal or the more powerful legends.

quotes.name: Loot, the Nexus
quotes.text: Loot, the Nexus is only guaranteed to tap for 1 mana, but with the potential to tap for 2, 3, or even more, it stands out as a premium green uncommon, particularly in Konstrari.

quotes.name: Unflinching Hortimancer
quotes.text: It’ll basically be unplayable outside of it, but that just means that when you’re drafting Vigorbloom, you should be able to take as many of these as you need.

quotes.name: Memory Trap
quotes.text: This is an early frontrunner for white’s best common, but even if it isn’t, it should still be a premium pickup when you’re drafting white.

quotes.name: Consign to Memory
quotes.text: While this is the best sideboard card in Modern for very good reasons, Consign to Memory is far too situational to see any Limited play.

quotes.name: Extrapolate the Impossible
quotes.text: Having so little agency over what you can get from Extrapolate the Impossible makes it look pretty unplayable from where I’m standing.

quotes.name: Way of the Cryomancer
quotes.text: That would lead me to believe that Way of the Cryomancer is unplayable, but there’s so much potential here that I’m doubting it.

quotes.name: Last Gasp
quotes.text: For 2 mana, this is one of the most efficient removal spells in FRA, and it’ll probably be the best black common.

quotes.name: Rampart Hunter
quotes.text: The ETB ability might be enough to warrant playing it in some decks, but this looks like filler material at best.

quotes.name: Refute Destiny
quotes.text: Even if you do only sideboard this, it’s probably the strongest card you’ll bring in for the right matchups.

quotes.name: Splinter Twin
quotes.text: On the one hand, it’ll be unplayable in most decks, but Reality Fracture does have a little twist in it.

quotes.name: Sphinx's Approach
quotes.text: I think this is quite playable in a slower control deck, but I’d never play it in an aggressive deck.

quotes.name: Hexhaven Battalion
quotes.text: It ended up widely regarded as the best white common and one of the best commons overall.

quotes.name: Hexhaven Battalion
quotes.text: This card looks amazing to me, and it’s my early pick for white’s best common.

themes.name: Evasion and stalls
themes.blurb: How a board that has stopped moving gets unstuck.

quotes.name: Undulating Witness
quotes.text: Fixing your mana is incredible, and you’ll sometimes play this just for that ability, then if you do happen to cast it, a big flying creature is hardly the worst thing to play.

quotes.name: Heartstring Puller
quotes.text: Turning one of those 2/2s into a 3/1 with trample, as Heartstring Puller is doing, raises the bar a fair bit and helps these two creatures to provide some extra utility over their predecessors.

quotes.name: Lyra, Archangel of Dawn
quotes.text: Sadly that’s not the case, but Lyra, Archangel of Dawn is still able to buff itself, which makes it a 3-mana 3/3 flying Ajani's Pridemate when white has access to a lot of sources of lifegain.

quotes.name: Sureshot Sower
quotes.text: When you draw it late it’ll get a lot worse, but the ability to discard it and destroy a flying creature gives it a great extra purpose when you get to that point in a game.

quotes.name: Ruric Thar, Biomagus
quotes.text: A huge flier that gets +2/+2 whenever you cast a noncreature spell and replaces itself if your opponent tries to target it is going to be pretty hard to deal with.

quotes.name: Mind Meanderer
quotes.text: I loved getting to play Affectionate Indrik back in Guilds of Ravnica , so give it flying and an extra ability and you know I’m still going to love it.

quotes.name: Medic's Kitesail
quotes.text: The ability to give a creature flying tends to be pretty strong, especially if you have a deck that might struggle with breaking out of a board stall.

quotes.name: Hunter's Axe
quotes.text: Much like an equipment that grants flying, granting trample is a huge bonus that helps your big, dumb creatures to get their damage through blockers.

quotes.name: Lyra, Tolarian Archangel
quotes.text: A 3/3 flier for 3 mana is already great, and if you ever get to activate its ability for 5 mana, you’re completely running away with the game.

quotes.name: Konstrari Charm
quotes.text: I honestly think this is leaning much closer to sideboard territory than anything else, and then you bring it in to attack flying creatures .

quotes.name: Aerid Konstrari
quotes.text: You don’t need much to sell me on a 5/4 with flying for just 4 mana, but yeah, I’ll take a few extra abilities while we’re at it.

quotes.name: Variable Chaser
quotes.text: A 2/3 with flying and prowess is a very good rate for a 3-drop, but it’s hard to see Variable Chaser as much more than that.

quotes.name: Ghalta the Unstoppable
quotes.text: An 8/8 with trample that gives trample to all your creatures is a lot more impactful than a glorified 7/7 vanilla creature.

quotes.name: Saheeli, Consul of Oversight
quotes.text: It’s also a huge flier, so even if you don’t have anything to trigger Saheeli right away, it’s not exactly a dead card.

mentions.text: Even sacrificing a creature to Silence the Echo won’t get you all the way there.
Black has two great cards that enable it in Silence the Echo and
Much like the Rank Rat , Tinybones, Pocket Nuisance is a good value card to give you some early card advantage while affecting the board.

It’d be quite nice to curve a turn-2 Rank Rat into a turn-3 Way of the Deathbringer , but this -2 ability isn’t always going to be as good as that, so this is one of the more mediocre enchantments in this cycle .
Technically this can work with Emrakul, the Exigent Doom , but to do that you’d have to play a land that doesn’t tap for mana.

quotes.name: Aerid Konstrari
quotes.text: Aerid Konstrari isn’t only a beefy creature that can close out games, it also ramps you with a Heartwood token and then has an activated ability that not only creates more of them but also speeds up the clock and kills your opponent faster?

quotes.name: Woodwork Prodigy
quotes.text: There are only a handful of cards in the set that create these hallmark tokens for Konstrari’s artifact ramp strategy, so having a card that can keep churning them out each turn sounds incredibly powerful to me.

quotes.name: Pia, Determined Rebuilder
quotes.text: You should play Pia, Determined Rebuilder in every red deck, but it’s Konstrari that will be able to utilize it the most, as they can give Pia the artifacts needed to activate its ability.

quotes.name: Hexhaven Invigorator
quotes.text: Even in Konstrari, where the Heartwood tokens would help to fix for it, there are going to be plenty of times when this will be stuck in your hand and you’re too far away from casting it.

quotes.name: Murmuring Volume
quotes.text: I don’t think Murmuring Volume quite stacks up against the rest of them, but it’s worth noting that Konstrari are trying to ramp with artifacts and this is definitely a way to do that.

quotes.name: Loot, the Nexus
quotes.text: Loot, the Nexus is only guaranteed to tap for 1 mana, but with the potential to tap for 2, 3, or even more, it stands out as a premium green uncommon, particularly in Konstrari.

quotes.name: Puppet Crafting
quotes.text: In the context of Reality Fracture , there are a good number of artifacts and enchantments for Puppet Crafting to combine with, including the Heartwood tokens out of Konstrari.

quotes.name: Konstrari Improviser
quotes.text: While this is obviously good in a Konstrari deck, the fact that this is hybrid red/green allows you to play it in a variety of decks that might also want an effect like this.

quotes.name: Gallia, Tragic Host
quotes.text: I’m very impressed however at Gallia, Tragic Host ’s potential inclusion in graveyard-centric decks like Theorix, where you can mill this satyr or discard it for value and then pull it out of the graveyard without costing anything from your hand or field.

quotes.name: Uldaros Theorix
quotes.text: Simply casting Uldaros gives you an immediate two/three-for-one depending on the situation, and if you’re filling your graveyard as we’ve seen that Theorix is very capable of doing, that just gives you a lot more options for what to do with it.

quotes.name: Cryotheory Adept
quotes.text: If you’re milling yourself aggressively in Theorix, then Cryotheory Adept is a great card to hit, since it actually does something relevant from the graveyard, while also being something you can play on the board if you draw it.

quotes.name: Arni, Humble Scribe
quotes.text: The fact that you can probably use it twice in a turn thanks to its creaturefall trigger will let you churn through your deck pretty quickly, which will be especially good in Theorix to fill your graveyard.

quotes.name: Consider
quotes.text: Fatehold will love it since it triggers all of its abilities, Theorix appreciates the help it gives you to load the graveyard, and the blue/red deck will also like it for triggering prowess.

quotes.name: Dark Matter Manipulator
quotes.text: Theorix is all about self-mill , so getting to mill three cards as early as turn 1 sounds like something they’ll be very interested in doing.

quotes.name: Liliana the Repentant
quotes.text: Theorix decks are going to love it, but any black deck apart from an aggressive Stingerquill one will be very happy to play this Liliana.

quotes.name: Seasoned Cryomancer
quotes.text: This puts you +2 on card advantage since you’re not spending a card, and you can even use it if you just mill it with Theorix cards.

quotes.name: Ajani Resolute
quotes.text: Vigorbloom is of course a lifegain archetype, but the fact that you need to have gained life at least three times before Ajani can use its -4 and survive makes me think this isn’t where we want to be.

quotes.name: Germinate Recruits
quotes.text: Vigorbloom has some great ways of gaining life, but they mostly cost a lot of mana, so paying 3 more to Germinate Recruits in the same turn sounds far too situational for my liking.

quotes.name: Enlightened Confidant
quotes.text: Having lifelink is a good way to help you with that, assuming you can attack with them, but it’ll be the other lifegain sources from Vigorbloom that will really let this pop off.

quotes.name: Blessed Ghoul
quotes.text: In Reality Fracture in particular, I think this is a great way to get value out of milling yourself and a cheap lifelink creature helps to trigger various Vigorbloom triggers.

quotes.name: Vigorbloom Vanguard
quotes.text: The point of lifegain, the vigilance, these aren’t the kinds of bonuses that can elevate Vigorbloom Vanguard beyond the level of a simple common, despite being uncommon.

quotes.name: Surgical Precision
quotes.text: It won’t do much early on, but you can always cycle it if you need to, and both modes gain you life too, making this an especially good inclusion in Vigorbloom decks.

quotes.name: Unflinching Hortimancer
quotes.text: It’ll basically be unplayable outside of it, but that just means that when you’re drafting Vigorbloom, you should be able to take as many of these as you need.

quotes.name: Liliana the Faultless
quotes.text: Considering we have Vigorbloom really wanting lifegain sources, Liliana the Faultless looks like an exceptional Soul Warden for that archetype to function.

quotes.name: Yuriko, Hope from the Shadows
quotes.text: Yuriko, Hope from the Shadows doesn’t do this particularly consistently, but it does also have the buyout of getting to surveil 2, which can also trigger Fatehold cards, so this ninja seems pretty good on balance.

quotes.name: Saheeli, Consul of Oversight
quotes.text: Creating a thopter token every time you scry or surveil is incredible in Fatehold, but it also synergizes incredibly with the Jace tokens, so it might just be good enough to top the curve in any white deck.

quotes.name: Consider
quotes.text: Fatehold will love it since it triggers all of its abilities, Theorix appreciates the help it gives you to load the graveyard, and the blue/red deck will also like it for triggering prowess.

quotes.name: Fatehold Charm
quotes.text: When looking over these charms , I figured Fatehold Charm would probably have Consider as one of its modes, so the mode of drawing a card and empowering 2 is a very nice surprise.

quotes.name: Diviner of Victory
quotes.text: Between its own prepared spell, Jace tokens, and the Fatehold archetype as a whole, Diviner of Victory may be able to attack as a 3/3 or even a 4/4 on certain turns.

quotes.name: Proctor of Potential
quotes.text: Getting to surveil without spending mana is going to really make the Fatehold deck come alive, and that’s exactly what Proctor of Potential does for you.

quotes.name: Denzilore Fatehold
quotes.text: Flash enables Denzilore Fatehold to swoop in during combat for an easy two-for-one, or just at the end of a turn to avoid sorcery-speed removal.

quotes.name: Fatehold Chronologist
quotes.text: You wouldn’t think I’d be interested in a Storm Crow , but Fatehold Chronologist is a great design to work well with its Peer Review spell.

quotes.name: Stingerquill Voxmancer
quotes.text: The Stingerquill archetype is based around sources of noncombat damage in the first place, and Stingerquill Voxmancer preparing itself every turn means it can give you noncombat damage every turn.

quotes.name: Master of Barbs
quotes.text: Normally, the ability on Master of Barbs would look kind of situational, but thanks to the Stingerquill prepared spell, Vicious Verse, there should actually be a lot of ways to trigger it.

quotes.name: Extended Absence
quotes.text: There’s a lot of good removal in Reality Fracture , but there’ll always be a need to cleanly remove anything, and the extra damage ping is very welcome in Stingerquill.

quotes.name: Cast Away Doubt
quotes.text: Cast Away Doubt ’s upside is quite relevant in Reality Fracture though, as the 2 damage to your opponent is perfect for triggering the effects of Stingerquill cards.

quotes.name: Whiplash Wordsmith
quotes.text: Stingerquill is probably the most aggressive archetype in Reality Fracture , so it’s far more interested in creatures that are cheaper than Whiplash Wordsmith .

quotes.name: Stinging Vitriol
quotes.text: Two mana is very reasonable for this effect, and you’ll always get the 2 damage out of it anyway, so it’ll also trigger your Stingerquill synergies.

quotes.name: Liliana the Repentant
quotes.text: Theorix decks are going to love it, but any black deck apart from an aggressive Stingerquill one will be very happy to play this Liliana.

quotes.name: Ingris Stingerquill
quotes.text: One of the keys to a good Stingerquill deck will be the ability to deal noncombat damage without spending any mana.

quotes.name: Jace's Machinations
quotes.text: On its own, Jace's Machinations is an instant that draws you two cards, since you can -3 the Jace token on your opponent’s turn and again on yours, leaving behind a Jace with 2 loyalty.

quotes.name: Protege's Awakening
quotes.text: Just like with Jace's Machinations , this could just be a simple draw spell in most blue decks, but one built around  utilize it so much more.

quotes.name: Jiang Yanggu, Alone
quotes.text: Jiang Yanggu, Alone , or to give him his proper title, Jiang Wick, is perhaps the victim of Jace’s gravest crime in creating the Echoverse.

quotes.name: Living Library
quotes.text: Living Library isn’t something I’ll go out of my way for, but it may be able to find a home in a good blue/green Jace deck.

quotes.name: The Theorist, Jace Beleren
quotes.text: All of the best planeswalkers protect themselves, and both of Jace’s main loyalty abilities are capable of doing that.

quotes.name: The Theorist, Jace Beleren
quotes.text: This is Jace’s set, so of course we get an incredibly powerful card to represent him.

quotes.name: Ajani Resolute
quotes.text: While Ajani Resolute is probably my favorite design in this set, answering the question “What would Ajani's Pridemate look like as a planeswalker ?”, it sadly feels very lackluster for Limited play.

quotes.name: Lyra, Archangel of Dawn
quotes.text: Sadly that’s not the case, but Lyra, Archangel of Dawn is still able to buff itself, which makes it a 3-mana 3/3 flying Ajani's Pridemate when white has access to a lot of sources of lifegain.

quotes.name: Ajani's Anguish
quotes.text: At the end of day, Ajani's Anguish is fine and you could use it better in a Konstrari ramp deck , but a lot of red decks aren’t going to be interested in playing it.

quotes.name: Unflinching Hortimancer
quotes.text: Ajani's Pridemate is a design that has proven itself time and time again in previous sets.

quotes.name: Titanbones, Towering Heart
quotes.text: Ajani's Pridemate is a tried and tested formula that really works.

quotes.name: Chandra's Emberling
quotes.text: I’d assume that Chandra's Emberling just isn’t good enough at first, though it wouldn’t be that shocking if it was playable.

quotes.name: Chandra, Chill of Compliance
quotes.text: Chandra’s Echoverse double has a lot to live up to.

quotes.name: Garruk, Curse Breaker
quotes.text: Then on future turns, whatever other big plays you make will draw you more cards without even using Garruk’s loyalty abilities.

quotes.name: Garruk, Curse Breaker
quotes.text: On top of that, we get a free Garruk's Uprising , which makes all the difference.

comparisons.text: Arcane Omens was incredible in Secrets of Strixhaven , but this is a very different format.

comparisons.name: Liliana the Faultless
comparisons.text: Considering we have Vigorbloom really wanting lifegain sources, Liliana the Faultless looks like an exceptional Soul Warden for that archetype to function.

comparisons.name: Lich's Relic
comparisons.text: We’ve just seen how relevant Crude Bent Blade ended up being in The Hobbit , only this time this is targeted removal, which means it’s going to be even better.

comparisons.text: We just had Gnashing of Teeth in The Hobbit , and Fulminous Forte looks remarkably similar.

comparisons.name: Ruric Thar, Magecrusher
comparisons.text: I was very high on Karakyk Guardian in Tarkir: Dragonstorm , and it turned out to be one of the best uncommons in the entire set.

comparisons.name: Simulacrum Shaper
comparisons.text: The classic Solemn Simulacrum always felt a little over-costed, but at 3 mana it’s absolutely perfect.

comparisons.name: Desperate Futurescribe
comparisons.text: Luminarch Aspirant is still one of the most broken rares we’ve seen in the last decade.

comparisons.name: Hapatra, the Desert Fang
comparisons.text: This reminds me a lot of Cloud of Darkness from Final Fantasy , one of the best uncommons in that set.

comparisons.name: Mind Meanderer
comparisons.text: I loved getting to play Affectionate Indrik back in Guilds of Ravnica , so give it flying and an extra ability and you know I’m still going to love it.

comparisons.name: Null Summoner
comparisons.text: Stealing an opponent’s card and then potentially getting to cast it for yourself is pretty busted, kind of like a Thought-Knot Seer crossed with Hostage Taker .

comparisons.name: Stingerquill Charm
comparisons.text: All three modes are incredible, especially with the base rate of just being Lightning Strike .

comparisons.name: Gideon's Memorial
comparisons.text: We can simply ignore the second ability and this is still an Intangible Virtue that you could also use as a mediocre removal spell.

comparisons.name: Hexhaven Battalion
comparisons.text: In Kamigawa: Neon Dynasty , there was a card called Imperial Oath .

comparisons.name: Memory Trap

comparisons.name: Teyo, Lightshield Expert
comparisons.text: Some, like Shardmage's Rescue , provide some additional benefit beyond stopping a removal spell, but Teyo, Lightshield Expert not only gives a +1/+1 counter (or loyalty counter), but a whole body for you to use to your advantage.

comparisons.name: Plan for All Outcomes
comparisons.text: It’s only sorcery speed, and that didn’t stop Trickster's Stratagem , but staying in play and letting you empower when you cast a noncreature spell each turn is incredible.

comparisons.name: Multiply by Zero
comparisons.text: As such, I was always puzzled by how Divide by Zero didn’t feel quite like the result of dividing by zero.

comparisons.name: Heartwood Crafter

comparisons.name: Yoshimaru, Beloved Companion
comparisons.text: When we’ve seen these kinds of effects in the past, like on Winding Constrictor or Conclave Mentor , they’ve been pretty strong.

comparisons.name: Fblthp, Impossibly Lost
comparisons.text: Fblthp, Impossibly Lost has a lot of text, but it basically amounts to a 2-mana spell that draws you two cards if you can deal combat damage to your opponent, kind of like when you cast Chart a Course .

comparisons.name: Semester Foreseer
comparisons.text: The comparison to make here is to Campus Composer , a pretty good card from Secrets of Strixhaven .

comparisons.name: Theorist's Proxy
comparisons.text: The empower 3 allows you to draw a card, which already makes Theorist's Proxy comparable to something like a Spirited Companion , but the high toughness also makes it better at protecting your Jace token should you need to build it up for a bigger loyalty ability.

comparisons.name: Gallia, the Merrymaker
comparisons.text: Two-drop creatures that can give haste to your other creatures entering, like Axgard Cavalry , have been reasonable in the past.

comparisons.name: Greenhouse Propagator
comparisons.text: Acting as both a mana dork and a Soul Warden , a lot of decks will be happy to run Greenhouse Propagator .

comparisons.name: Traxos, Scourge Eternal
comparisons.text: Needing you to cast a creature or artifact spell to untap it is a pretty big downside, but unlike the original Traxos, Scourge of Kroog , Traxos, Scourge Eternal at least enters untapped, so you get that first attack without needing to cast another spell.

comparisons.name: Blessed Ghoul
comparisons.text: I’ve always been a big fan of Sanitarium Skeleton , so swapping out that second point of toughness for lifelink sounds like a fair trade.

comparisons.name: Ajani Resolute
comparisons.text: While Ajani Resolute is probably my favorite design in this set, answering the question “What would Ajani's Pridemate look like as a planeswalker ?”, it sadly feels very lackluster for Limited play.

comparisons.name: Sphinx's Approach
comparisons.text: This is simply a Quick Study that’s harder to cast, which is just barely still good enough.

comparisons.name: Bloodline Recollector
comparisons.text: This is a real far cry from Emeritus of Ideation .

comparisons.name: Hexhaven Invigorator
comparisons.text: Just like its black counterpart, Phyrexian Obliterator , this isn’t remotely good enough.

comparisons.name: Hexhaven Dueling Arena
comparisons.text: I thought Skycoach Waypoint might have been good enough, but it ended up being pretty bad, so I imagine the same is true here.

comparisons.name: Roiling Canopy
comparisons.text: A green-shifted Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle is kind of cool, but Roiling Canopy does literally nothing until you reach your sixth forest in play.

high.name: Ajani Unrelenting
high.text: I’m assuming that you’ll use the -3 ability a lot of the time you play Ajani, and the fact that you get the Cadet token as well as wiping the board seems truly absurd.

high.name: Chandra, Torch of Defiance
high.text: When it was originally printed in Kaladesh , it was an absolute house in Standard and was basically the best card in the format up until it rotated.

high.name: The Theorist, Jace Beleren
high.text: All of the best planeswalkers protect themselves, and both of Jace’s main loyalty abilities are capable of doing that.

high.name: Lyra, Tolarian Archangel
high.text: This is a truly absurd rare, and I expect to lose to it quite a bit in this format.

high.name: Overwrite the Multiverse
high.text: While Sunfall was one of the best cards in March of the Machine , Overwrite the Multiverse will likely fall short of that.

high.name: Aerid Konstrari
high.text: This card is absolutely incredible and a great first pick to cement you into what might be the best Hexhaven school.

high.name: Stingcaster Mage
high.text: The best thing to do will typically be to flashback a removal spell and turn this into a makeshift Flametongue Kavu , but there are a lot of other options.

high.name: Seasoned Cryomancer
high.text: It’s still pretty good though, and the best ability it has is the last one, where you can draw two cards by exiling it from your graveyard.

high.name: Tenured Tethermage
high.text: There are a bunch of creatures in Reality Fracture that ramp you for 3 mana, but Tenured Tethermage might be the best of the lot.

high.name: Null Summoner
high.text: Stealing an opponent’s card and then potentially getting to cast it for yourself is pretty busted, kind of like a Thought-Knot Seer crossed with Hostage Taker .

high.name: Bloombrute
high.text: I often say that the best build around cards in Limited are usually the ones that draw a card whenever you do the thing, so of course I like Bloombrute .

high.name: Fulminous Forte
high.text: That extra bit of flexibility over a sorcery makes a big difference and sells this to me as one of red’s best and most versatile cards.

low.name: Roiling Canopy
low.text: That won’t happen unless you warp your entire draft around forcing mono-green, so since it enters tapped, that makes it strictly worse than a forest and you should never play it.

low.name: Extrapolate the Impossible
low.text: Not only should all your best cards be in your main deck already, but your opponent gets to give you the worst option of the two you show them.

low.name: Root Maze
low.text: Root Maze is absurdly bad and you should never play it.

low.name: Consign to Memory
low.text: While this is the best sideboard card in Modern for very good reasons, Consign to Memory is far too situational to see any Limited play.

low.name: Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun
low.text: I view Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun as basically nothing more than a vanilla 2/1, which you should basically never play.

low.name: Ferocity of the Hunt
low.text: That sounds amazing when you frame it that way, but that’s only the best-case scenario.

low.name: Wrecking Gecko
low.text: Naturally, as a common, Wrecking Gecko is the worst by a lot.

low.name: Germinate Recruits
low.text: This is a 1/10 in most scenarios and a 10/10 when it works.

low.name: Way of the Necromancer
low.text: It’s not unplayable, but it’s definitely not good.

low.name: Rampart Hunter
low.text: The ETB ability might be enough to warrant playing it in some decks, but this looks like filler material at best.

low.name: Sphinx's Approach
low.text: I think this is quite playable in a slower control deck, but I’d never play it in an aggressive deck.

low.name: Konstrari Charm
low.text: Gruul Charm was abysmal and now Konstrari Charm is easily the worst of this cycle.
